newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-EU flexes muscles on Boeing/McDonnell merger.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-EU flexes muscles on Boeing/McDonnell merger.

text.p: In its strongest language to date, the European Commission warned Boeing Co on Tuesday that it would block its proposed $14 billion merger with McDonnell Douglas Corp unless European concerns about the deal were met.

Only one week before it is expected to make a final ruling on the agreement, the Commission said Boeing had not yet made enough proposals to address its concerns about the impact of the deal on competition.
It also formally backed the tough stance taken against the merger by its antitrust chief, Commissioner Karel Van Miert.

"The (Commission) fully supported the position taken by Mr Van Miert thoughout the negotiations," Commission chief spokesman Nikolaus van der Pas said in a statement that was unprecedented in a merger case.
"Unless the legitimate competition concerns of the Commission can be met and genuine choice maintained for purchasers of aircraft worldwide, the Commission could not approve the merger," he said.
Boeing said it still hoped for an agreement.

"We believe that the proposals put forward (by Boeing) are an honest effort to meet the Commission's concerns. I'm hopeful there will be a deal," Jim Frank, Boeing's vice president for European affairs, told Reuters.

The Commission has the power to block the deal under EU law which gives it jurisdiction over mergers and takeovers involving companies with a combined worldwide turnover of five billion European currency units ($5.5 billion) and 250 million Ecus each in sales in the 15-nation bloc.
Were Boeing to ignore a ruling against it, the Commission could fine it up to 10 percent of its turnover and fine any European companies doing business with the U.S. aviation giant.
Commission sources said that in the event the EU could also seize any new planes being delivered in Europe.

The statement on Tuesday removed any doubts about the EU's determination to resist warnings from the other side of the Atlantic that a ban would cause a damaging political row between the two trade partners.
Industry sources and antitrust lawyers believe that Boeing will not run the risk of being shut of the European market, which accounts for 30 percent of the world's total aircraft orders.

Their betting is that Boeing, which would increase its share of the civilian aircraft with more than 100 seats to 70 percent from 64 percent and see its customer base jump to 84 percent from 60 percent through the merger, will negotiate.
But like other large multinationals which faced similar fights with the EU in the past it may wait until the last minute to do so.
"I believe Boeing will test the Commission's patience until July 22," an industry source said, referring to the day before the Commission is expected to take its final decision.
The Commission's statement said that Boeing had not met its concerns the merger would strengthen its dominant position and harm fair competition in the EU.
"Boeing has so far not agreed to measures which would meet these concerns," it said.

National antitrust experts from the EU's 15 states will meet on Wednesday for the second time on the merger. They unanimously backed the Commission's position on July 4 that the deal should be banned in its current form.
Boeing shares were little changed by Tuesday's news.

Boeing's negotiations with the Commission have focused on controversial long-term exclusive supply pacts signed between the aircraft manufacturer and U.S. airlines AMR Corp's American Airlines, Continental Airlines and Delta Air Lines; concerns that Boeing will automatically replace McDonnell Douglas planes which account for 25 percent in the fleets worldwide; and the danger that defence contracts money will spillover to Boeing's commercial business.
McDonnell Douglas makes mainly military aircraft.
The U.S. Federal Trade Commission cleared the deal without conditions earlier this month.
